transcript.text: Worcester Greenstar 30i combi - pressure keeps dropping to about 0.5 bar every few days and I have to top it up. Can you help me work out why?

A sealed combi system should not need regular topping up. Dropping from normal pressure to about 0.5 bar every few days means water is escaping somewhere, either visibly or via the boiler’s safety discharge.

For a Worcester Greenstar 30i, set the pressure to roughly 1.0–1.3 bar when the system is cold. It will usually rise somewhat when hot, commonly to around 1.5–2.0 bar.

## Most likely causes

### 1. Expansion vessel issue / pressure relief valve (PRV) discharging
This is very common.

If the expansion vessel has lost its air charge or failed, system pressure rises excessively as the heating warms up. Once it gets to around 3 bar, the PRV opens and releases water through a copper pipe to outside. When everything cools down again, the pressure is low.

Typical pattern:
• Cold pressure: around 1–1.3 bar after topping up
• Heating on: pressure climbs unusually high, perhaps above 2.5 bar or towards 3 bar
• Later, when cold: pressure has dropped markedly
• Water/drips from the small copper discharge pipe outside, often near the boiler’s flue or external wall

Check: After the boiler has been running for an hour or two, look at the end of that external copper pipe. It should be dry. If it is dripping or leaves wet marks, call a Gas Safe registered heating engineer. They will check/recharge or replace the expansion vessel and may need to replace the PRV too.

Do not block or cap that pipe.

### 2. Small leak on the heating system
A tiny leak can lose enough water over several days without making an obvious puddle.

Check, with the heating cool if possible:
• Radiator valve spindles and valve unions
• Towel rails, especially around valves and bleed points
• Pipework beneath radiators
• Any visible pipes at the boiler
• Damp patches around floors, ceilings, skirting boards or cupboards
• Green/white staining or corrosion around valves and joints

Also check whether a radiator bleed screw is weeping. Avoid repeatedly bleeding radiators unless there is actually trapped air, as bleeding releases water and lowers pressure.

### 3. PRV not sealing properly
Even if the pressure has not risen to 3 bar recently, a PRV can sometimes fail to reseat after operating and then drip slowly outside. Again, the external copper discharge pipe is the key check.

### 4. Leak inside the boiler
Less commonly, there can be an internal leak from a pump seal, automatic air vent, heat exchanger, or another component. This may not be visible without removing the boiler casing, so that is an engineer job.

## Useful test to do over the next day

1. With the boiler cold, top it up to about 1.2 bar.
2. Take a photo of the pressure display/gauge.
3. Run the heating and note the pressure once fully hot.
4. Check the external PRV discharge pipe for dampness/dripping.
5. Check the pressure again the following morning when cold.

This helps distinguish the likely fault:

| What happens | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| Pressure shoots up towards 3 bar when hot, then falls after cooling | Expansion vessel / PRV |
| Pressure steadily falls whether heating is on or off, external pipe dry | Leak somewhere in heating circuit or boiler |
| External PRV pipe drips even at normal pressure | Faulty PRV |
| Pressure rises by itself while boiler is off | Filling loop/filling valve may be passing — though this usually causes pressure to rise, not fall |

## What to do now

• Keep it around 1.0–1.3 bar cold; don’t overfill it.
• Don’t keep topping it up indefinitely: repeated fresh-water top-ups introduce oxygen and can accelerate corrosion/sludge in the system.
• Arrange a Gas Safe heating engineer if it is losing pressure every few days. Tell them: “Greenstar 30i losing pressure from about 1.2 bar to 0.5 bar every few days; please check PRV discharge, expansion vessel and for system leaks.”
• If the boiler is under Worcester Bosch warranty, use Worcester Bosch or an approved service engineer, as this may be covered depending on the warranty terms.

If you tell me how high the pressure gets when the heating is fully hot, and whether the external copper discharge pipe is wet, I can narrow it down quite a lot.

Thanks. When the heating's on full it goes up to nearly 3 bar, then drops again. And yes, the little copper pipe outside the wall drips sometimes, more when the heating's on. No gas smell and my CO alarm hasn't gone off.

That strongly points to a failed or discharged expansion vessel, with the pressure-relief valve (PRV) then releasing water outside.

What is happening:

1. You top up the cold system to normal pressure.
2. When the heating warms the water, it expands.
3. The expansion vessel should absorb that expansion, but likely has lost its air charge or its internal diaphragm has failed.
4. Pressure rises towards 3 bar.
5. The boiler’s PRV opens to protect the system and discharges water through that outside copper pipe.
6. Once cold, there is less water left in the system, so the pressure falls — and you need to top it up again.

The external dripping is therefore an important confirmation. The PRV may also continue to seep afterwards, even once the expansion vessel fault is fixed, because debris or wear can stop it resealing fully.

## What to do

Arrange a Gas Safe registered heating engineer to inspect it soon. Tell them:

> “Worcester Greenstar 30i: pressure rises to nearly 3 bar when heating is on, the PRV discharge pipe outside drips, and pressure falls to 0.5 bar every few days.”

They will normally:
• Check the expansion vessel’s air charge and whether its diaphragm has failed
• Recharge the vessel if it is sound, or replace it if not
• Check/replace the pressure-relief valve, particularly if it still drips after the repair
• Check the filling loop and system for any additional leaks

It is not a gas leak symptom, and your CO alarm would not normally be involved in this type of fault. The boiler’s safety valve is doing its job, but repeated topping-up is not good long term: fresh water introduces oxygen and minerals, increasing corrosion/sludge risk.

## Until it is repaired

• Keep the cold pressure only around 1.0–1.2 bar; do not fill it higher.
• Avoid running the heating hard for long periods if possible, as it will drive the pressure up and dump more water.
• If it reaches 3 bar, turn the heating off and let it cool rather than continuing to run it.
• Do not cap, block, or alter the outside copper discharge pipe.
• If the boiler loses pressure completely, shows a fault code, leaks internally, or water is coming from anywhere other than the discharge pipe, switch the heating off and seek prompt help.

This is usually a routine repair rather than a boiler replacement issue.
